title: De Natura et Origine Animae
author: Augustine

passages.original: dum meminisse nos et intellegere et uelle certissimi sumus, qui nos naturae nostrae magnos cognitores esse iactamus quid ualeat memoria nostra uel intellegentia uel uoluntas omnino nescimus. amicus quidam meus iam inde ab adulescentia, Simplicius nomine, homo excellentis mirabilisque memoriae, cum interrogatus esset a nobis, quos uersus Vergilius in omnibus libris supra ultimos dixerit, continuo celeriter memoriterque respondit. quaesiuimus etiam superiores ut diceret: dixit. et credidimus eum posse retrorsus recitare Vergilium; de quocumque loco uoluimus, petiuimus ut faceret: fecit.
passages.english: While we are most certain that we remember and understand and will, we who boast that we are great knowers of our own nature have no idea at all what our memory or understanding or will can do. A certain friend of mine from adolescence onward, Simplicius by name, a man of excellent and wonderful memory, when he was asked by us what lines Virgil had spoken in all [his] books just before the last ones, immediately answered quickly and from memory. We asked him also to say the ones before those: he said them. And we believed that he could recite Virgil backwards; from whatever place we wished, we asked him to do it: he did it.
passages.notes: "in omnibus libris" probably means in each of the books (i.e. the lines preceding the last line of every book). "supra ultimos" is taken as "before the last lines".
